description: Leviathan is a satellite-based flood detection and analysis system. We use NASA radar imagery, image processing algorithms, and machine learning to detect flooding by comparing satellite data over time. Our system maps affected areas, identifies potentially damaged roads and infrastructure, and provides engineers and emergency responders with data to make faster, more informed decisions.
summary:
Leviathan is an interactive global map that uses radar imagery from the NASA–ISRO NISAR mission to show how floods change Earth's surface. Users can explore NISAR coverage anywhere in the world, select an area, and compare radar images taken on different dates. Radar sees through clouds and at night, so it can observe floods when ordinary satellite photos can't. Calm water reflects the radar signal away from the satellite, so newly flooded ground appears darker.

For each analyzed area, users can swipe between before and after images, view a map of where the surface changed, highlight areas that may have flooded, and see which roads crossed those areas. A "How we know" panel lists the source images, their dates, our processing steps and what the data can't confirm.

Leviathan makes complex radar data readable for engineers, emergency managers, scientists and the public worldwide. By connecting satellite evidence to roads and communities, it helps people decide where to look first after a flood. It also stays honest about what remains uncertain.
details:
Leviathan is an Earth-observation evidence explorer built for the "Dancing with the SARs" challenge. It turns real NASA–ISRO NISAR products into interactive, inspectable studies of surface change: users discover a study, explore earlier and later radar acquisitions on a live map, inspect measured change (Δσ⁰ backscatter, ΔSM soil moisture, unwrapped InSAR phase, pixel offsets), and trace every number back to its source granule, processing method and validation status.

Benefits/impact: SAR products are powerful but hard to trust and interpret — Leviathan makes the evidence chain visible, separating measured values from interpretation and marking provisional vs validated products honestly, so scientists, responders and non-specialists can rely on radar data. Four real studies are connected: Louisiana coastal backscatter (GCOV), Louisiana soil moisture (SME2), Louisiana interferometric phase (GUNW, honestly kept in radians) and West Greenland ice motion (GOFF) — over 41.5 million valid measured samples from 6 NISAR granules.

Tools: React 19 + TypeScript + Vite frontend, MapLibre GL interactive maps (Esri World Imagery basemap), Python/h5py/pyproj offline pipeline that downloads, subsets and renders granules into static evidence assets, deployed on Vercel. Creativity: a static-first "evidence explorer" rather than a black-box analysis server — quality masks, provenance and honest unit/claim boundaries are first-class UI, not footnotes. We considered scientific honesty (no displacement/velocity claims the data can't support), accessibility for non-SAR users, and no implied NASA endorsement.
